title: FSLogix Deep Dive: Profile Containers, Cloud Cache, and Storage
summary: FSLogix is the profile layer that makes non-persistent AVD and Windows 365 desktops feel personal. This lesson goes deep on the two container types, the critical VHDLocations-vs-Cloud-Cache decision, how to wire Azure Files to Entra-joined hosts with Microsoft Entra Kerberos, sizing and exclusion tuning, and how to read FSLogix's status/reason/error codes when a profile won't attach.
objectives: Explain the difference between a Profile Container and an Office Container (ODFC) and when to use each
Choose between VHDLocations and Cloud Cache for profile storage and explain why the two are mutually exclusive
Configure Azure Files as FSLogix profile storage using Microsoft Entra Kerberos authentication for Entra-joined session hosts
Apply sizing, exclusion, and performance best practices for profile containers at scale
Diagnose common FSLogix failure modes, including locked VHDX files, using FSLogix status, reason, and error codes
Decide between per-machine and per-user FSLogix agent installation for a given host pool design

quiz.q: What is the primary difference between a Profile Container and an Office Container (ODFC) in FSLogix?
options: ODFC is the only container type that supports Azure Files; Profile Container requires local disk
Profile Container is deprecated in favor of ODFC for all new deployments
ODFC stores registry hives while Profile Container stores only documents
Profile Container holds the entire user profile (NTUSER.DAT, AppData, etc.); ODFC optionally splits out just the Office/OneDrive cache data into a second VHD(X)
quiz.why: Profile Container is the primary, full-profile container (registry hive, AppData, desktop, etc.). ODFC is an optional, separate container that isolates Outlook/OneDrive cache data — useful when you want Office data on faster or differently-sized storage, or when combining with other profile solutions. Both can attach to the same or different storage locations.

quiz.q: Which two settings are mutually exclusive in an FSLogix profile configuration?
options: VHDLocations and Cloud Cache — a configuration uses one or the other, not both
SizeInMBs and IsDynamic — you must pick a fixed or dynamic disk, never configure size
ODFC and Outlook — you cannot use FSLogix with Outlook at all
Profile Container and folder redirection — folder redirection is required with FSLogix
quiz.why: VHDLocations points FSLogix at one or more plain storage paths in priority order, while Cloud Cache is a separate replication engine that asynchronously mirrors the profile across up to four locations for high availability and DR. An FSLogix configuration uses one mechanism or the other, not both simultaneously.

quiz.q: Your session hosts are Microsoft Entra joined only (no on-premises Active Directory, no Microsoft Entra Domain Services). Which authentication method lets them mount an FSLogix profile share on Azure Files without line-of-sight to a domain controller at logon time?
options: NTLM authentication with a local storage account admin
Microsoft Entra Kerberos authentication for Azure Files
Azure AD Domain Services joined to the same VNet
Anonymous SMB access with share-level permissions only
quiz.why: Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Microsoft Entra ID issue the Kerberos tickets an Entra-joined (or hybrid-joined) session host needs for SMB access to an Azure Files share — no domain controller or Microsoft Entra Domain Services required for the sign-in path. You still need one system with AD line-of-sight once to assign the share-level RBAC and NTFS permissions, but session hosts themselves don't need it at runtime.

quiz.q: A user's FSLogix log shows the profile failed to attach with a Windows system error 0x00000020 (ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION) on the VHDX file. What is the most likely cause?
options: The storage account has run out of capacity
The user's Microsoft Entra token has expired
The user's VHDX is already open — an active or orphaned session elsewhere still holds a lock on the file
The VHDX file format is corrupted beyond repair
quiz.why: ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION (0x00000020 / decimal 32) is the classic Windows error for 'file in use by another process' — in FSLogix terms, another session (active, disconnected-but-not-cleaned-up, or on a different host) still has the VHDX mounted. First checks: look for the user's other active sessions across the host pool, then check for stale locks.

quiz.q: An April 2026 Windows Server update changes a Kerberos default that can break FSLogix access to SMB file shares if they haven't been upgraded first. What is that change?
options: SMB 1.0 is removed entirely from Windows Server
Kerberos is replaced by certificate-only authentication
The default session ticket lifetime is reduced to 5 minutes
The default Kerberos encryption type changes from RC4 to AES-SHA1
quiz.why: Microsoft's FSLogix documentation flags that the April 2026 Windows Server update changes the default Kerberos encryption type from RC4 to AES-SHA1. File shares hosting FSLogix containers that haven't already been upgraded to AES-SHA1 can see access failures once that update lands, so it needs to be handled proactively, not reactively.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, explain when you would choose Cloud Cache over a single VHDLocations path on Azure Files with Zone-Redundant Storage (ZRS), and name one real trade-off of using Cloud Cache.
quiz.answer: Cloud Cache is the right choice when you need multi-region or multi-provider redundancy and automatic session-host failover — for example, replicating a profile across an Azure Files share in one region and a file server share in another, or supporting active-active disaster recovery, since Cloud Cache can replicate to up to four locations and fail over automatically if the primary is unreachable. A single VHDLocations path with Azure Files ZRS is simpler and sufficient when you only need protection against a single datacenter/zone failure within one region. The trade-off with Cloud Cache is added complexity and local cache disk requirements on each session host (a local cache directory is needed for the asynchronous replication), plus more moving parts to monitor and troubleshoot than a single VHDLocations target.
quiz.why: Cloud Cache trades simplicity for resilience: it's the documented approach for FSLogix HA/DR beyond what a single storage target with platform-level redundancy (like Azure Files ZRS) can offer, but it requires local cache storage per host and adds operational complexity that a straightforward VHDLocations deployment doesn't have.

body_markdown:
## Why FSLogix Matters

Any non-persistent host pool — the pooled, multi-session model that makes AVD and Windows 365 Frontline cost-effective — has a hard problem: the operating system disk is thrown away or reset between sessions, but users expect their desktop, their pinned apps, their Outlook signature, and their browser bookmarks to follow them every time. FSLogix solves this by storing the user's profile in a virtual disk file that mounts at logon and detaches at logoff, so pooled hosts feel personal without ever persisting user data on the host itself. It's the single most consequential storage decision you'll make in a VDI deployment, and it's directly examined under AZ-140 Domain 3.

## Profile Container vs. Office Container (ODFC)

FSLogix ships two container types. The **Profile Container** is the primary one: it holds the entire user profile — the NTUSER.DAT registry hive, AppData, Desktop, Documents, Favorites, everything Windows considers 'the profile.' Most deployments need only this.

The **Office Container (ODFC — Office 365 Container)** is optional and narrower: it isolates just the Outlook OST cache and OneDrive data into a second VHD(X). You'd reach for ODFC when you want Office data to live on different, faster storage than the rest of the profile, when you're layering FSLogix with another profile tool that already manages the base profile, or when Outlook cache growth is large enough that you want to manage its lifecycle independently. In most modern AVD builds, a single Profile Container is sufficient — reach for ODFC only when you have a specific reason.

## VHDLocations vs. Cloud Cache — Pick One

This is the decision every AVD/Windows 365 architect has to make explicitly, and it's binary: **an FSLogix configuration uses either `VHDLocations` or Cloud Cache, never both.**

- **`VHDLocations`** is a simple, ordered list of one or more UNC paths. FSLogix tries each path in order until it finds (or creates) the user's container. Pair this with a storage backend that already provides redundancy — Azure Files configured for Zone-Redundant Storage (ZRS) is the standard 2026 pattern — and you get resilience against a zonal failure without any FSLogix-side complexity.
- **Cloud Cache** is a different engine entirely. It asynchronously replicates the profile across up to four storage locations simultaneously — for example, an Azure Files share in one region plus a file server share in another — and automatically fails a session host over to a healthy location if the primary becomes unreachable. Cloud Cache is the documented path for multi-region HA/DR scenarios that a single storage target can't cover on its own. The trade-off: Cloud Cache needs local cache disk on every session host for the asynchronous write-back layer, and it adds real operational surface area — more logs, more failure modes, more to monitor.

Rule of thumb for the exam and for production: if platform-level redundancy (ZRS, geo-redundant file server clustering) covers your resilience requirement within one region, use `VHDLocations`. If you need cross-region failover or multi-provider redundancy, use Cloud Cache.

## Storage Backends: Azure Files with Entra Kerberos, or Azure NetApp Files

Azure Files is the default recommendation for FSLogix storage — good cost-to-management ratio and it's compatible with both Active Directory Domain Services and Microsoft Entra ID identity models. For session hosts that are **Microsoft Entra joined only** (no domain controller, no Microsoft Entra Domain Services), enable **Microsoft Entra Kerberos authentication** on the storage account: go to the storage account, **File shares → Identity-based access**, and select **Microsoft Entra Kerberos**. This lets Microsoft Entra ID issue the Kerberos tickets your Entra-joined hosts need for SMB access — no domain controller line-of-sight required at sign-in. You still need one machine with AD line-of-sight once to grant the RBAC role (Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor or similar, scoped per user/group) and configure NTFS permissions on the share.

For customers with heavier IOPS/throughput needs or who are already invested in NetApp, **Azure NetApp Files** is the alternative — but note it currently requires session hosts to be joined to Active Directory Domain Services (or Microsoft Entra Domain Services), not Entra-joined-only.

One 2026 operational note worth flagging now and revisiting in Module 6: an April 2026 Windows Server update changes the **default Kerberos encryption type from RC4 to AES-SHA1**. File shares hosting FSLogix containers that haven't already been upgraded to AES-SHA1 can see logon-time access failures once that update rolls out — this is a proactive fix, not a wait-and-see one.

## Sizing, Exclusions, and Performance

Use **dynamically expanding** VHD(X) files (the FSLogix default) rather than fixed-size — they only consume as much storage as the profile actually uses. Set a generous `SizeInMBs` ceiling (30,000 MB / ~30 GB is a common starting point) since dynamic disks won't pre-allocate it. Exclude noisy, regenerable folders from the profile with the standard FSLogix exclusion list — browser caches, `%LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Teams`, `AppData\Local\Temp` — to keep container growth under control. Keep your FSLogix storage share in the **same Azure region** as your session hosts to minimize latency, and separate it from any App Attach file share (Module 5, Lesson 2) since the two workloads have different I/O patterns.

## Reading Failure Modes: Status, Reason, and Error Codes

FSLogix records three values per user session in the registry: a **Status** code (Normal or Error), a **Reason** code that explains a *Normal* status (for example, `REASON_LOCAL_PROFILE_EXISTS` or `REASON_WINDOWS_TEMP_PROFILE`), and a Windows **Error** code that explains why an operation failed — these are standard Windows System Error Codes, not FSLogix-invented numbers. The most common one you'll see in the field is `0x00000020` (`ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION`, decimal 32) — the file is already open elsewhere, almost always because the user has another active or orphaned session holding the VHDX lock. Status code `12` (`ERROR_ATTACH_VHD`, "Can't attach to virtual disk") is the general attach-failure bucket you'll see wrapping that underlying error. Your first move on any attach failure is always the same: check the profile log at `C:\ProgramData\FSLogix\Logs\Profile\Profile_<user>.log` for the underlying Windows error, then check for other sessions/locks before touching permissions.

## Per-Machine vs. Per-User Install

FSLogix is installed per-machine (once per session host image, applied to all users) in the overwhelming majority of AVD and Windows 365 deployments — it needs to run before any user profile loads, which a per-user install can't guarantee. Bake the agent and its registry configuration into your golden image (Module 3) so every new session host is FSLogix-ready from first boot.

Enable it on the storage account under File shares, Identity-based access. Entra ID then issues the Kerberos tickets your hosts need at sign-in. You still need one machine with AD line-of-sight once, to grant the RBAC role and NTFS permissions on the share itself.

Exclude noisy, regenerable folders like browser caches and Temp directories to keep growth under control. And keep your storage share in the same Azure region as your session hosts to minimize latency.

slides.title: Reading a Failed Attach
bullets: Status, Reason, and Error codes are stored per session in the registry
Error codes are real Windows System Error Codes, not invented
0x00000020 ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION = VHDX locked elsewhere
Check the Profile_<user>.log for the underlying Windows error first
slides.narration: When a profile won't attach, FSLogix leaves you three values: a status code, a reason code, and — critically — a Windows error code, because these come from real Windows System Error Codes, not something FSLogix invented. The one you'll see most often in the field is error 0x00000020, sharing violation, meaning the file is already open somewhere else. Always start by reading the Profile log for that underlying Windows error before you touch permissions.

slides.title: Locked VHDX: The Classic Failure
bullets: Sharing violation means another session still holds the file
Check for the user's other active sessions across the host pool first
Then check for stale, orphaned locks from crashed sessions
Permissions are rarely the actual cause of this specific error
slides.narration: The locked VHDX is the classic FSLogix support call. A sharing violation means another process, almost always another session for that same user, still has the file open. Your first move is checking whether the user has an active session elsewhere in the host pool. Your second move is checking for a stale lock left behind by a session that crashed instead of logging off cleanly. Permissions are rarely the real cause of this particular error.

slides.title: Per-Machine, Not Per-User
bullets: FSLogix must run before any user profile loads
Install per-machine in the golden image, not per-user
Bake the agent and registry config into every new host
Consistent, image-level install avoids a whole class of bugs
slides.narration: One last practical point. FSLogix has to run before any user profile even starts loading, so it's installed per-machine, baked into your golden image, not deployed per-user. Every new session host that comes from that image is FSLogix-ready from first boot, which avoids an entire category of inconsistent-configuration bugs. Next lesson, we move from storing the profile to delivering the applications inside it: App Attach.
